words.meaning: to study something again before a test

words.meaning: the ability to understand what you read or hear

words.meaning: to add short notes to a text while reading
words.example: The students annotated the poem with their own comments.

words.meaning: to keep delaying something you must do
words.example: Don't procrastinate — start your essay today.

words.meaning: the ability to keep information in your memory
words.example: Sleep improves the retention of new vocabulary.

words.meaning: to think of many ideas quickly, often in a group
words.example: The class brainstormed ideas for the school project.

words.meaning: to give the main points of something briefly
words.example: Summarize the article in three sentences.

words.meaning: to say something again in your own words
words.example: Paraphrase the paragraph instead of copying it.

words.meaning: a test that checks what someone knows or can do
words.example: The final assessment covers everything we studied.

grammar.title: 3A: Choosing between comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation:
Use **comparative adjectives + than** to compare two people, places, or things. You can compare two tutors, or decide which textbook is better for you.

Short adjectives take **-er**: tall → **taller**, big → **bigger**. Longer adjectives use **more**: modern → **more modern**, and one-syllable adjectives ending in -ed use **more** too: tired → **more tired**.

Three adjectives are irregular: good → **better**, bad → **worse**, far → **further** (or **farther**). A good assessment score always feels better than a bad one.

Use **(not) as + adjective + as** to say two things are equal. You can also say two things are **the same as** each other.

Comparative adverbs compare two actions: fast → **faster**, slowly → **more slowly**. Well → **better** and badly → **worse** are irregular.

Use **the + superlative** to compare one thing with all of its group: **the tallest**, **the most expensive**, **the best**, **the worst**. Your best retention comes from the most active study methods.

After a superlative, use **in** (not of): the best beach **in** the world. We often use a superlative with the present perfect + **ever**: the best book I have **ever** read.

Choose the comparative for two things and the superlative for one thing in a whole group. Ask yourself: which habit helps your comprehension most?

Superlatives work for study tips too: the best way to revise, the most useful way to annotate, the fastest way to summarize.

Compare your own habits honestly: do you brainstorm ideas before you write, or do you procrastinate? Can you paraphrase a chapter in your own words?
examples: My new tutor is *more patient than* my old one. (comparative adjective + than)
Revising with flashcards is *easier than* rereading the chapter. (comparative adjective + than)
Her reading comprehension is *better than* mine. (irregular comparative)
I learn *more slowly than* my classmates, but I remember longer. (comparative adverb)
Don't annotate *as quickly as* you read — slow down. ((not) as + adverb + as)
He procrastinates *more than* anyone I know. (comparative adverb)
Testing yourself gives *better* retention *than* rereading. (irregular comparative + than)
Brainstorming alone is *less fun than* brainstorming with friends. (comparative)
She can summarize a chapter *faster than* the teacher can. (comparative adverb)
Try to paraphrase *as clearly as* the original author. ((not) as + adverb + as)
This was *the hardest* assessment *in* the whole course. (superlative + in, not of)
It is *the best* study method I have *ever* tried. (superlative + present perfect + ever)

practice.q: Which is correct: 'This book is more interesting than that one' or 'This book is interestinger than that one'?
practice.a: The first one. Long adjectives use more, never -er.

practice.q: Fill the gap: She is ___ student in the class. (good)
practice.a: the best — use the superlative with the for one person in a whole group.

practice.q: Is 'the best beach of the world' correct?
practice.a: No — say 'the best beach in the world'. Use in, not of, after a superlative.
